words.asking: Discuss asks for several distinct considerations, each named and then carried one step further to its consequence for the people in the vignette. It is the outline's most common verb and it nearly always arrives with a number attached — two liquidity considerations, two governance concerns — so the marks sit on how many separate points you raise, not on how deeply you develop any one of them. A discuss answer is a short list of independent claims, each with a because.
highlight: Name the consideration in the first few words of each point, then spend one sentence on its consequence here; a bank grading key accepts a point only when the reasoning is attached.
Use the vignette's own facts as the because — the 25% private equity allocation, the move from 4% to 5% spending. The same point stated in the abstract is what keys call vague.
Write exactly the number of points asked for, as separate blocks, since credit is awarded per point and a merged paragraph makes the second point hard to find.
leaveOut: Extra points beyond the number requested. Graders take the first two, so a weak point placed first costs a mark that a later strong one cannot win back.
Background definitions of the instruments involved. Discuss assumes you already know what private equity or an LDI hedge is.
A recommendation, unless the stem asked for one. 'I would therefore cut PE to 10%' earns nothing on a discuss item and costs you minutes.

shape.length: Two to four sentences per requested point. Four-point items almost always want two points and six-point items three, so budget roughly half the marks to each block.
shape.structure: One labelled block per point: the consideration, then its consequence for this portfolio.

workedExample.note: Its key lists eight acceptable liquidity considerations and pays full credit for any two that carry reasoning. Capital-call risk earns the point because it is paired with 'investment-grade fixed income is fully invested, so private equity introduces timing uncertainty'; the bare claim that private equity is illiquid does not.

pointLosers: Restating the stem as the first point — answering 'what liquidity considerations arise' with 'the portfolio becomes less liquid'.
Two versions of one idea. Unpredictable capital calls and lumpy distributions are usually read as a single liquidity-timing point, so the second block scores nothing.
Burying the consideration at the end of a paragraph of setup, where a grader scanning for the named point will not find it.

confusedWith.difference: Describe wants the mechanics of one thing in order; discuss wants several independent considerations, each only one step deep.
Explain wants one causal chain followed to its implication; discuss wants breadth across separate reasons, and depth on any single one is unpaid.

words.asking: Describe asks you to lay out the features or the mechanics of one specific thing — a strategy, a structure, a process — in enough operational detail that someone could act on it. The marks are in the moving parts: which instrument, which direction, which maturity, in what order, sized by what rule. No opinion is wanted here and none is scored.
highlight: The concrete mechanics: instrument, direction (long or short, pay-fixed or receive-fixed), tenor, and the sizing rule.
The order of the steps, when the thing being described is a process. A good describe answer reads like instructions.
Any constraint the stem bolted on — 'without compromising the hedge' — because keys usually reserve a mark for honouring it.
leaveOut: Why the strategy is a good idea. That is justify, and on a describe item it is unpaid writing.
The alternatives you considered and rejected.
Definitions of the instrument class. Nobody scores 'a futures contract is an agreement to buy at a future date'.

shape.length: Four to six sentences or bullets on a four-point item — enough to name every moving part once, with no sentence spent on merit.
shape.structure: Name the thing, then its components in the order they are put on, then the constraint that shapes the sizing.

workedExample.note: The key pays for naming the steepener and sizing it so the LDI hedge survives: long two-year futures, short ten-year, DV01-neutral, run as an overlay at a modest share of total PV01. Its partial-credit line drops the answer that merely identifies the strategy, because the identified label is not the description.

pointLosers: Naming the trade and stopping. 'Put on a curve steepener' is the heading, not the answer.
Describing the market view instead of the position that expresses it.
Leaving direction ambiguous. 'Use two-year and ten-year futures' never says which leg is long, so the grader cannot award the mechanics mark.

confusedWith.difference: Describe stops at how the thing is built; explain has to reach why it produces the result, so it needs a causal sentence describe does not.
Describe goes deep on one item's mechanics; discuss spreads across several considerations and would lose marks for that much detail on one.

words.asking: Explain asks for the causal chain behind something: why this leads to that. One mechanism, followed through to what it means for the portfolio, is the whole answer. The scored words are the connectives — because, therefore, which means — and the grading keys generally want the chain to arrive at a consequence for the manager rather than stopping at a definition.
highlight: The mechanism in one sentence and its consequence in the next: this happens, therefore the manager must do that.
The distinction the question rests on, stated outright before you use it, such as market sensitivity versus sensitivity to rewarded factors.
The portfolio implication. An explain answer that ends where the definition ends is the one that takes partial credit.
leaveOut: A second, alternative mechanism. Explain pays depth in one chain, not a list of candidate causes.
Numbers, unless the stem asked you to calculate. Working the arithmetic is not the explanation.
Hedged phrasing like 'this may or may not matter', which reads to a grader as not knowing the mechanism.

shape.length: Three to five sentences on a four-point item: the distinction, the mechanism, the implication. Roughly half the marks hang on the last of those.
shape.structure: Cause, then effect, then what the effect obliges the portfolio to do.

workedExample.note: Full credit needs the definition, the mechanism, and the attribution logic; the key's partial-credit line pays only part for the two definitions on their own. The last mark comes from following the chain out — returns attributable to factor exposure have to be stripped out before anything left over is called alpha.

pointLosers: Stopping at the definition. This is the single most common way an explain answer leaves its final mark unclaimed.
Explaining the concept in general when the stem pointed at one fund, one client, or one balance sheet.
Offering three shallow reasons where one developed chain was wanted; none of the three reaches the implication.

confusedWith.difference: Describe lists the parts; explain has to connect them, so an explain answer must contain a because that a describe answer does not need.
Discuss is graded on how many separate considerations you raise; explain is graded on whether one chain reaches its consequence.

words.asking: Evaluate hands you somebody else's claim, recommendation, or system and asks you to judge it. Every item named in the stem gets a verdict — correct, incorrect, does not comply, a strength, a weakness — and one reason that makes the verdict stick. The verdict is what gets marked and the reason is what protects it. Where the stem says three claims, the grader is counting three verdicts, and a claim you never assess scores nothing however good the prose around it is.
highlight: A one-word verdict on each item before any reasoning, so a grader can find all of them without reading for them.
The single reason that decides each verdict, stated in the vignette's terms: factor strategies concentrate exposure rather than diversify it.
Verdicts on the items that are right as well as the ones that are wrong. Keys pay for correctly leaving a sound claim alone.
leaveOut: A general essay on the topic the claim touches. Evaluate is about the claim, not the subject.
A fix for whatever you judged wrong, unless the stem also said recommend.
Unresolved hedging. 'Partially correct' with nothing after it reads as no verdict at all.

shape.length: One short block per item: verdict, then a sentence of reasoning. Three claims in a six-point item means three blocks of roughly equal weight.
shape.structure: Item, verdict, reason — repeated in the order the vignette introduced them.

workedExample.note: The key marks each of the three claims separately and says full credit requires spotting the first as the only incorrect one. The two correct claims still need a verdict and a supporting line, so an answer that only attacks the wrong claim has answered a third of the item.

pointLosers: Assessing the claims you find interesting and skipping one, which caps the item at partial credit no matter how strong the rest is.
Calling a claim wrong without naming the specific error, which the keys treat as an unsupported verdict.
Judging every claim the same way. These items usually mix correct and incorrect on purpose, so a clean sweep in either direction is a warning sign.

confusedWith.difference: Discuss raises considerations and never has to land on a verdict; evaluate is unmarkable without one.
Evaluate judges a position someone else took; justify defends the position you took, so the reasoning points the other way.

words.asking: Recommend asks for an action specific enough to hand to someone to carry out, plus the line that ties it to this client's situation. It almost never travels alone: the outline bolts it to a second verb (recommend and justify an asset allocation, identify the biases and recommend methods to overcome them), and no stem in the bank opens with it. So the action is one half of the marks and the setup verb is the other, and the half you skip is simply lost.
highlight: Enough specificity to act on — which instrument, how much, over what horizon, at what participation rate.
The sentence linking the action to the client's stated constraint. That link is what turns a plausible action into the recommended one.
The other verb in the stem, answered first and in its own block, since the challenges you identify and the strategy you recommend are marked in different places.
leaveOut: A menu of options. A recommendation is one course of action; naming three and leaving the choice open answers nothing.
Best practice that never touches this portfolio's numbers.
A re-derivation of the diagnosis you already wrote under the first verb.

shape.length: Two blocks on a four-point item: the setup verb's answer, then the action with its rationale in three or four lines.
shape.structure: Diagnosis, then the action in the imperative, then one line on why it fits the constraint.

workedExample.note: The key wants the challenges first — the order is two-thirds of average daily volume in a small cap with a wide spread — and only then the action, specified down to spreading it over three to five days at a capped participation rate across both lit and dark venues. Its partial line rejects naming a single algorithm, which is the recommendation with the sizing left out.

pointLosers: Recommending the category. 'Use an algorithm' or 'diversify' skips the parameters, which is where the marks are.
Answering the recommend half and skipping the identify or evaluate half that came first.
Proposing something the vignette's own constraints rule out, such as completing in one day an order that is most of a day's volume.

confusedWith.difference: A determine answer is forced by the facts and can be marked right or wrong; a recommend answer is a course of action you propose and have to sell.
Select picks from the closed list the vignette supplies; recommend may propose an action that appears nowhere in the stem.
Recommend earns marks for the action, justify for the because. An item asking for both scores them in separate places, so neither covers for the other.

words.asking: Compare sets two or more items against each other on the same dimensions, with both the common ground and the divergence visible. The keys reward taking each item through the same short list of properties and then stating the difference outright. An answer that describes the first item fully, then the second fully, and never puts them side by side leaves the comparison marks unclaimed even when every fact in it is right.
highlight: Choose the two or three dimensions before you start writing — cost, downside, upside cap — and take every item through all of them.
State the difference in its own sentence: the put costs premium and creates a floor, the call collects premium and creates a ceiling.
Where the stem names a client objective, finish by saying which item fits it. On these items a mark usually rides on that sentence.
leaveOut: A third strategy the stem did not name, however relevant it feels.
Full pricing mechanics of each instrument; compare is about relative behaviour, not valuation.
Any dimension you can only fill in for one of the items, since a one-sided row proves nothing about either.

shape.length: Two short blocks, one per item, then a differences block — around eight lines for a four-point item.
shape.structure: Item A on the chosen dimensions, item B on exactly those dimensions, then the explicit contrast and the fit to the stated objective.

workedExample.note: The key runs the protective put and the covered call through identical dimensions — premium direction, maximum loss, upside treatment — and only then adds a key-differences block: one protects and costs, the other pays and does not protect. The closing mark goes to picking the put for a client whose stated focus is downside.

pointLosers: Two sequential descriptions with no shared dimension, leaving the grader to do the comparing.
Comparing on a dimension the vignette gives no data for, which reads as padding.
Skipping the recommendation when the stem handed you a client objective to decide against.

confusedWith.difference: Compare keeps the similarities in; under contrast they earn nothing, so the same material written for compare wastes half its lines.
Discuss lets each point stand alone; compare requires every point to be a shared dimension that both items are measured on.

words.asking: Justify is the because half of an answer. It is rarely alone — eight of the ten statements in the outline that use it read 'recommend and justify' — and it asks you to defend one specific choice against the alternatives on the table, using the criterion the vignette named. Wording like 'support your answer' or 'explain your choice' is asking for exactly this and is marked in the same place: the choice on its own usually earns partial credit, and the rest arrives with a reason tied to the client's criterion.
highlight: The client's own criterion as the hinge — cost minimisation, a shortfall constraint, a near-term liquidity need.
Why the alternative loses, in one clause. A defence that never mentions the rejected option is half an argument.
Numbers you already computed, reused as the evidence: a net credit of $2.70 against a $2.37 outlay is the justification, not the preamble to one.
leaveOut: A second independent reason. Keys accept any one sound reason, so the spare is unpaid.
The mechanics of the option you chose, which is describe wearing a justify label.
Generic merit — 'it is well diversified' — with no tie to the stated objective.

shape.length: One or two sentences per justification, attached to the choice it defends. Where the stem pairs justify with another verb, expect roughly half the marks on each.
shape.structure: The choice, then the criterion, then how the choice meets it and the alternative does not.

workedExample.note: The pick is the bear call spread, and the key's ladder gives only part credit for naming it. The rest comes from the reason: that spread is entered for a net credit while the alternative needs cash up front, and the client asked to minimise cost. Both payoff tables exist only to produce that one comparison.

pointLosers: Choosing correctly and stopping. This is the most common way to leave half of a justify item unclaimed.
Justifying against a criterion you introduced rather than the one the vignette stated.
Writing the defence of an option you did not pick, so the verdict and the reasoning point in different directions.

confusedWith.difference: Recommend supplies the action; justify supplies the argument for it. A stem carrying both needs both blocks written.
Evaluate delivers a verdict on somebody else's claim; justify defends your own choice against the alternative you rejected.
Explain traces a mechanism that holds whatever you choose; justify argues that this option beats the named alternative for this client.

words.asking: Contrast is compare with the similarities cut out. Only differences score, and each one has to be a real axis of divergence — a property on which the two items behave in opposite ways — not two unrelated facts placed next to each other. It is rare in the outline and usually paired with identify, and the bank's differences items are graded on how many distinct axes you name with both sides filled in.
highlight: One axis per point, both sides stated: one method reads actual positions, the other regresses returns on style indexes.
Differences that change what the analyst can do — whether position transparency is required, how fast style drift shows up.
The requested number of differences and no more, each written so it stands alone without the one above it.
leaveOut: Similarities, however true. Under contrast they are unpaid.
A verdict on which item is better, unless the stem asked for one.
A second difference that is the first one renamed. Accuracy and precision on the same axis count once.

shape.length: One or two sentences per difference with both sides named; two differences on a four-point item, three on a six-point one.
shape.structure: Parallel pairs — on this axis A does one thing and B does the other — repeated for each axis.

workedExample.note: Every line of its key is a two-sided pair: actual positions against a regression on style indexes, a point-in-time snapshot against an average over the estimation window, drift visible at once against drift that lags. Any two of those pairs earn full credit, while the one-sided version — that holdings-based analysis is more accurate — is what the key scores as vague.

pointLosers: One-sided statements that give a property of A and never say what B does instead.
Opening with what the two approaches have in common, which spends a line that cannot be paid.
Listing five differences when two were asked for, so the strongest one may sit outside the two that get read.

confusedWith.difference: Compare wants similarities and differences on shared dimensions; contrast wants the differences only, so shared ground is a line you do not write.
Describe develops one item's mechanics in depth; contrast needs both items on every point, so depth on one side is half an answer.

words.asking: Identify asks for the name of the thing — the bias, the violation, the measure, the risk — in as few words as it takes to be unambiguous. It is a cheap verb that rarely stands alone: every statement in the outline that uses it pairs it with a second verb, and 25 of the 35 essays in the bank that use it do the same, so most of the marks sit downstream in the interpreting, contrasting, or evaluating. Even a pure identify item, though, wants a clause saying why the thing qualifies here.
highlight: The name first, in terms a grader can match against the key: survivorship bias, Standard VII(B), the rebalancing cost of equal weighting.
One clause grounding it in the vignette, because keys score a bare label as vague.
Exactly the number asked for, each genuinely distinct — two facets of one issue are marked once.
leaveOut: Development past that clause, unless a second verb asked for it. The time belongs to the paired verb.
Fixes and implications, which are recommend and explain.
A hedged list. 'Possibly survivorship bias, or perhaps the short history' names nothing.

shape.length: One or two lines per item: two items for four points, three for six.
shape.structure: A short labelled line per item — the name, then the clause that grounds it.

workedExample.note: Eight issues are acceptable and any two earn full credit, but the key pays nothing for vague ones. 'Survivorship bias' works because the expected clause is there — failed firms leave the index and inflate its history. Note that the five-year sample and the equal weighting are separate issues, while a short history and too few business cycles are one issue twice.

pointLosers: Naming the category instead of the item: 'a data problem' where the key expects survivorship bias.
Listing four when two were asked for, so a wrong first entry displaces a right one.
Writing a paragraph per item, which earns nothing extra here and starves the paired verb where the marks actually are.

confusedWith.difference: Identify names the thing and stops; describe has to lay out how it works, which is several sentences more.
Discuss carries every point one step to its consequence; identify leaves it at the name plus a grounding clause.

words.asking: Determine asks for the answer the facts force: a value, a named portfolio, a yes or no on compliance. There is one right answer and the grader checks it first, so the verdict carries a large share of the marks and the working or decisive fact carries the rest. Only about a quarter of the bank's determine items involve arithmetic; the others turn on one fact in the vignette. Either way nothing here is a matter of opinion.
highlight: The verdict on its own line, first: the portfolio number, the cost, does not comply.
The working laid out so that a slip still shows the right method, since keys award for correct method with an incomplete answer.
The one fact that settles a yes-or-no determination — two large near-term withdrawals shorten the horizon, so a more aggressive stance fails suitability.
leaveOut: The alternatives you ruled out, beyond a clause each. A determine item is not a comparison.
What should be done about the finding, unless the stem asked.
Qualified verdicts. 'Arguably complies' cannot be marked either way.

shape.length: Verdict then support, inside half a page. Four-point items typically split the marks between the answer and the work behind it.
shape.structure: Answer first, then the calculation or the decisive fact, then one line of interpretation.

workedExample.note: The key opens with the verdict and then computes the safety-first ratio for all three portfolios, because the ranking is the justification. Its ladder is the lesson: the right portfolio with thin work still scores well, the right portfolio for the wrong reason scores less, and the wrong portfolio picked on a 'safest' argument still earns something for reading the goal correctly. Compliance-style determine items read the same way with the decisive fact in place of the arithmetic.

pointLosers: Showing the working and never stating the conclusion in a sentence a grader can circle.
Computing the metric only for the candidate you favour, which leaves the ranking unproven.
Answering a compliance determination with a description of the standard instead of a verdict on the conduct.

confusedWith.difference: Determine has one defensible answer that the facts decide; recommend has a course of action you choose and then have to sell.
Both end in one named answer, but determine's is compelled by a metric or a rule, while select's is the best fit among options offered.

words.asking: Select asks you to pick one option from a list the vignette has already laid out, and to make the pick unmistakable. It is the rarest verb in the outline — one statement, which asks you to evaluate liability-based strategies across rate scenarios and then choose one that meets the portfolio's objective — and that is how it behaves in general: the evaluation is groundwork, the choice is the answer. Discussing all the candidates without landing on one scores nothing at all.
highlight: The chosen option named exactly as the vignette names it, on its own line.
The property that made it fit the objective: the largest security count for replication, the duration closest to the liability.
One clause on each rejected candidate, which is what shows the pick was reasoned rather than guessed.
leaveOut: Any candidate the stem did not put on the list.
A hedged pick. 'Either the second or the third would work' is not a selection.
A full description of every option. The evaluation serves the choice; it is not the product.

shape.length: The choice in one line, then two to four lines of support drawn from the exhibit.
shape.structure: Named choice, the deciding property, then the brief reason each alternative loses.

workedExample.note: No stem in the bank uses select, so this is the closest-shaped item: choose one of three debt indexes to track and defend it. The key names the winner, accepts any one supporting property (most securities, value weighting, a middle duration), and then lists separately the reasoning it rejects — which shows the pick is graded before the argument for it.

pointLosers: Evaluating all the candidates thoroughly and never naming one.
Picking on a property the exhibit gives no data for.
Changing the pick partway through the answer, which reads as no answer.

confusedWith.difference: Select is bounded by the options given; recommend can propose an action nobody in the vignette mentioned.
Determine's answer is the one the metric or rule compels; select's is the best fit for the objective among the options on offer.
